projects.title: Ozera
projects.description: A full-stack platform designed for LLM researchers with a focus on interpretability that lets users experiment on and visualize the internal mechanics of large language models as they generate text. It provides two from-scratch transformer LLMs alongside many open-source models, with tools for activation patching, attention head analysis, sparse autoencoder experimentation, custom model training, and publication-ready figure exports.Key Features:• Real-time layer-by-layer activation, attention, embeddings, and logit visualization during inference• Activation intervention & patching playground to test causal hypotheses about model behavior• Automated attention head classification (induction, copying, positional, sink) and pattern mining• Sparse autoencoder analysis, feature browsing, and cross-model feature comparison• Custom model training pipeline with dataset upload, cost estimation, and GPU job tracking• Credit-based access to compute for model training, inference, and experiments• Publication-ready figure export with NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML formatting presetsTechnical Implementation:• Models: Two transformer-based LLMs and corresponding sparse autoencoders built from scratch (no ML frameworks, just math)• Frontend: React 18 / TypeScript with D3, Plotly, Recharts, and Visx for interactive activation and attention visualizations• Backend: FastAPI with Supabase for authentication and PostgreSQL database, plus Stripe for credit-based billing• Compute: Serverless GPU inference on Modal using PyTorch and HuggingFace Transformers, with forward hooks• Deployment: Vercel for frontend, Railway for backendLive at: ozera.app

projects.title: Enfora
projects.description: A full-stack web application that combines financial commitment with AI validation to help users achieve their goals. Users create tasks with optional monetary stakes, and AI validates completion evidence through advanced document and image analysis.Key Features:• AI-powered evidence validation using OpenAI API (analyzes screenshots, PDFs, and documents)• Automated payment processing via Stripe for failed task accountability• Global leaderboard with proprietary reliability scoring algorithm• Recurring task support with smart deadline tracking• Two-factor authentication with TOTP, email codes, and backup codes• Real-time analytics tracking completion rates, streaks, and discipline metricsTechnical Implementation:• Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router• Backend: Node.js/Express REST API with JWT authentication• Database: AWS DynamoDB with GSI indexing and composite keys• Cloud Infrastructure: AWS Lambda (serverless task expiration), EventBridge Scheduler (automated deadline triggers), S3 (evidence storage), SES (email notifications)• Integrations: OpenAI API, Stripe API, Redis (rate limiting & caching)• Security: bcrypt password hashing, refresh token rotation with reuse detection, express-rate-limit with Redis backend, CSRF protection• Deployment: Vercel for frontend, Railway for backendArchitecture Highlights:• Event-driven task expiration with automatic payment charging• Serverless leaderboard caching (Lambda runs every 10 min to rank users)• AI validation pipeline with metadata verification to prevent cheating• Webhook-based payment reconciliation for transaction status updatesLive at: enfora.app (BETA)

projects.title: Jamify
projects.description: Jamify is an AI-powered web application that curates personalized Spotify playlists based on user-provided descriptions. Leveraging Python, Flask, the Spotify Web API, and the OpenAI API, the project interprets natural language inputs to search for music recommendations that align with user preferences and moods. The application is deployed on Heroku, ensuring seamless accessibility without the need for complex infrastructure management.Key features of Jamify include:- AI-Powered Playlist Generation: Utilizes the OpenAI API to analyze and interpret user inputs, transforming them into tailored search terms that are fed into the Spotify Web API.- Spotify Web API Integration: Retrieves search terms and track data from user inputs to generate playlists dynamically based on user preferences.- Web-Based Interface: Built with Flask to provide an intuitive and responsive user experience.- Error Handling & Robustness: Implemented thorough error handling mechanisms to manage API failures and edge cases.- Deployment on Heroku: Ensuring smooth and cost-effective deployment without the need for manual infrastructure management.The project was developed using Visual Studio Code IDE, taking advantage of its powerful debugging and development tools. Additionally, Flask-Mail was integrated to facilitate whitelist requests, enabling secure user authentication workflows via email.Check out Jamify here: https://bit.ly/jamifyNote: Due to limitations in Spotify Web API's development mode, access to the playlist generation is limited to users on a whitelist. However, getting on the whitelist is simple. Open Jamify in your browser, log in through Spotify, attempt to generate a playlist, and then enter your Spotify email to be added to the whitelist.

projects.title: LungSense.AI
projects.description: LungSense.AI is a specialized web application that leverages artificial intelligence to provide users with a clear, data-driven confidence score indicating their potential risk of lung cancer. By answering a brief yet intuitive questionnaire, users receive a personalized analysis based on health and environmental factors associated with lung cancer risk.The development involved significant technical and research-driven efforts. I started by creating a custom dataset tailored specifically for the model's training and testing needs. Instead of relying on publicly available datasets on Kaggle, which often lacked meaningful correlations between features and outcomes, I developed a rule-based dataset generation algorithm. This algorithm incorporated weighted features, biases, and mathematical relationships grounded in extensive research on the key contributors to lung cancer risk.The model development process was rigorous, as I had several machine learning algorithms trained, fine tuned, and validated through cross validation, grid search, and gradient-based optimization techniques. Ultimately, a Logistic Regression model was selected as the final model due to its superior performance in accuracy and reliability.I implemented the model into the backend by writing an API in Flask, enabling robust API functionality for processing user inputs and delivering real-time predictions. To maintain simplicity and scalability, no database was used, as user inputs are processed in real-time.I then created a seamless and efficient user experience on the frontend in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Designed for simplicity and accessibility, ensuring users could easily navigate the questionnaire and understand the results. To make the application widely accessible, it was deployed on Heroku, leveraging its scalability and ease of integration. DISCLAIMER: This project does not provide medical diagnosis, and is simply a showcase of machine learning development.

projects.title: Stock Predictor
projects.description: A machine learning based algorithm that predicts whether the index price of the S&P 500 will increase or decrease tomorrow or during the next trading period.The algorithm uses thousands of days of data from previous index prices of the S&P 500 provided by Yahoo Finance to make a prediction. It then cleans through the data using the Pandas Python library to prepare it for the machine learning algorithm. The algorithm trains a Random Forest Classifier model from Scikit Learn using a backtesting function on the data. The model is then improved upon using additional predictors to further increase accuracy.

Thrilled to share that our paper has been accepted into ACL SRW 2025! I look forward to presenting our work this week at the #1 ranked NLP conference in the world: ACL 2025 in Vienna, Austria. Our paper investigates whether large language models of different sizes converge on similar internal concepts. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and similarity metrics like SVCCA and RSA, we analyzed and quantified feature universality between Google 's Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models. Our results reveal novel multi-token subspace similarity, validate strong alignment of semantic features in the mid-layers of both models, and provide evidence that LLMs carve the world into broadly similar, interpretable features regardless of scale. We hope these findings move us closer to building cross-model interpretability tools and improving LLM safety and control through a deeper understanding of shared internal representations. A huge thank you to my incredible co-authors: Daniel Son , Sanjana Rathore , Andrew W. Rufail , Daniel Zhang , and Soham Dave , as well as our mentors Cole Blondin, Kevin Zhu , and Sean O’Brien for their guidance throughout this research effort. ...more

Excited to share that I've officially wrapped up my summer internship with Bixby Capital Management ! Over the past few months, I rotated through the acquisitions, investor relations, operations, property management, and accounting departments, which gave me a front row seat to how a commercial real estate deal actually comes together, from initial underwriting all the way through the end of due diligence. That work included compiling quarterly market reports from brokerage research, reviewing lease comps and estoppels, and touring investment properties. Getting to see the industrial asset side of the industry from so many different angles was an incredibly valuable learning experience, and I couldn't be more grateful. For my capstone project, I researched agentic and generative AI adoption opportunities across every department at the firm. I dug into where AI could realistically fit into everyday workflows without disrupting how the team already operates, and I presented my findings and recommendations to the entire company during my last week. Standing up in front of the whole firm and having people actually engage with my ideas was a moment I won't forget. The highlight of my summer, though, was the team itself. Everybody at Bixby, no matter their role or how busy they were, made time to teach me about what they do, what they were working on, and why it mattered. I never once felt like I was just shadowing people, I felt like I was actually part of the team. That kind of culture is rare, and it's clear that the people at Bixby are what make the firm so special. I'm leaving this internship with a much clearer sense of how the commercial real estate industry works as a whole, and an even clearer sense of the kind of team I want to be a part of going forward. Thank you, Bixby Capital Management , for an amazing summer! #CommercialRealEstate #Internship #ArizonaStateUniversity

As I enter the last week of my internship at LinkedIn , I wanted to look back on what I’ve accomplished and share some of the biggest things I’ve learned along the way. For the past 12 weeks, I’ve been building AI agents that help LinkedIn engineering teams understand and optimize their Microsoft Azure spend, alongside Olaoluwa James-Owolabi , Taeeun Kim , and my manager, Shweta Sahni . 1) Being a good teammate means more than just “doing your tasks.” Working on a team means everyone has their own responsibilities, but I learned pretty quickly that being a good teammate goes beyond just getting your own work done. Sometimes that means slowing down to review someone else’s code, moving faster when someone is waiting on you, communicating when you’re blocked, or putting your own task aside for a little while to help unblock someone else. 2) Working in a large codebase means learning what already exists before building something new. We were contributing to a codebase with over a million lines of code, and one of my biggest takeaways was how important it is to understand how similar problems have already been approached before jumping into your own solution. That meant looking through existing code, speaking with other teams, and making sure what I was building was up to the same quality as the code already in production. 3) AI works best when the problem is clearly defined. AI can write quality code and documentation quickly, but it can also go off track just as fast if the task isn’t clearly defined. I learned to break larger stories into smaller, well-defined tasks and spend more time upfront thinking through the approach and refining the plan before any code was written. Being deliberate about what I wanted to build, questioning assumptions along the way, and using AI to help execute led to better code, cleaner pull requests, and a stronger understanding of everything I was shipping.

Last night we won first place at SpaceXAI ‘s Grokathon 🔥🔥 We wanted to answer the question: If we gave agents all the tools that security professionals use to reverse engineer binaries, can we let grok reverse engineer decade old binaries made for gameboys and others platforms? Turns out we can :) We built a custom harness that allowed grok to reverse engineer binaries via static analysis, memory inspection + debugging, and dynamic computer use interaction. We were able to rewrite old gameboy ROMs up to 262kb in size to standard C, which then allowed us to remix and reimagine games. We posted our app on X and other platforms and received 2500 views and ~130 verified users in 12 hours. We even took this a step further. We found a 1995 BMW’s engine control unit’s (ECU) ROM, performed static analysis on it and built a clean-room implementation that allowed us to analyze the engine control signals during steady state operation. Since no existing emulator can properly simulate the ROM, we used what we learned from static analysis to patch an existing open source emulator, and was able to fully emulate the 1995 ROM initial cranking sequence. Shoutout to my awesome teammates Theo Chapman and Supratik Panuganti . Yall are the goats 🐐 #hackathon #grokathon

As my internship at LinkedIn wraps up in the next couple weeks, I wanted to take the time to reflect on my experiences and growth this summer. This summer, I worked on LinkedIn's Python Infrastructure team where I helped build an AI-powered autofixer that automatically converts Linkedin's Python services to safe async patterns, optimizing a previously tedious and error-prone migration across thousands of services. This internship taught me that software engineering ≠ coding. With the rise of agentic coding, many developers (including myself) have wondered what the future of software engineering looks like. But some of my biggest lessons this summer came from everything surrounding the code: navigating massive codebases, familiarizing myself with foreign systems, and making design decisions with real tradeoffs. I learned that great engineering isn't about just writing clean code, but also involves understanding the problem and designing the right solution. A big thank you to my tech lead Friedrich Ewald and manager Kaiyang Zheng for giving me the opportunity to contribute to a high impact initiative at LinkedIn and encouraging me to stay curious as I grow as an engineer. I'd like to also thank the rest of my intern pod, Anson Lam , Grace Jin , Emma Bennett for working alongside me, I couldn't have asked for a better group to learn, brainstorm, and navigate through the summer. Last but not least, a huge shout out to my recruiter Jeffery C. and the rest of the intern program team for planning super fun events that made this summer unforgettable! #LinkedInterns
